name: Stable chlorotic sectoring / suspected genetic variegation
summary: Sharply bounded chlorotic or chlorophyll-deficient sectors can be consistent with somatic mutation or mosaicism in Cannabis, but no published Cannabis image morphology proves genetic cause; treat this as an exclusion-based phenotype until serial lineage evidence and appropriate laboratory work support the attribution.
affectedParts: successive leaves from one shoot or meristem
whole plant only when a documented cultivar trait is established
stages: flowering; stage specificity is not established
indicators: Abrupt yellow, cream, pale-green, or near-white tissue adjoining normally green tissue within the same leaf
Sector-shaped or longitudinal pigment loss rather than uniform whole-leaf yellowing
The same shoot position or clonal lineage is mapped across successive leaves and time rather than inferred from one detached leaf
Affected tissue retains its boundary while new observations document whether the pattern remains localized, expands, disappears, or is joined by distortion and stunting

Record whether pigment loss remains sharply sectoral or becomes diffuse spotted bleaching; experimentally induced pigment-gene silencing also produced white or yellow spots, so pigment loss is mechanism-nonspecific

Record localized bleaching on the originally affected leaf separately from pigment loss in newly formed leaves; experimental TRV-mediated PDS silencing was largely restricted to treated leaves, so localization alone is not a genetic discriminator
Matched images preserve upper and lower leaf surfaces, whole-plant distribution, branch identity, scale, cultivar, developmental stage, and camera-lighting conditions
exclusions: Validated testing detects a virus or viroid consistent with the sampled tissue and syndrome
Mosaic, mottling, line patterns, curling, brittle growth, shortened internodes, stunting, or reduced inflorescence performance progress beyond the original sector
Chlorosis follows leaf age, interveinal or marginal patterns, or a measured tissue-nutrient, substrate-pH, or root-zone-EC abnormality better than a branch lineage
Microscopy or organism sampling confirms thrips, mites, leafminers, or another pest associated with the marks
The distribution maps to a lamp, spray, pesticide, plant-growth regulator, abrasion, heat event, or other documented exposure
A negative targeted pathogen assay or an unaffected-looking clone is the only basis for declaring a genetic cause or pathogen freedom
Pale and green tissues have been pooled or collected from different plants so the observed sector cannot be linked to the laboratory or genetic result
Localized pigment loss is attributed to a stable mutation solely because it remains confined to one leaf; experimentally induced gene silencing can also be localized
Camera white balance, glare, shadow, senescence, or cultivar pigmentation explains the apparent color boundary

progression.description: Capture calibrated whole-plant, branch, upper-surface, and lower-surface views; assign a symptom-only chlorotic-sector label, not a genetic ground-truth label.

Mark the shoot and record successive leaves and any cuttings over time. A stable lineage association increases suspicion of a developmental or genetic origin but does not exclude latent or localized infection.

The Divina/Pilar abstract reports lower leaf chlorophyll and generally slower growth in the named variegated cultivar under comparable long days. Record longitudinal growth and pigment measurements separately from sector imagery; this is not a same-leaf symptom progression or an image-only diagnosis of the cause.
Compare matched healthy tissue and evaluate pests, root-zone pH and EC, nutrient status, exposure history, and a region- and facility-appropriate virus/viroid panel before narrowing the cause.

Use genetic or meristem-lineage analysis when a genetic claim matters. Cannabis somatic mosaicism has been sequenced within one mother plant, but published evidence does not establish a universal visible phenotype or inheritance rule.

lookAlikes: Mosaic, mottling, or line-pattern syndrome of unresolved cause
Lettuce chlorosis virus or other regional virus
Iron, manganese, magnesium, or nitrogen disorder
Experimentally induced pigment-gene silencing in documented research material; not a diagnosis of natural TRV disease
Camera color, glare, or shadow artifact
confirmation: Distinguish untreated, empty-vector, and target-silenced research controls, keeping phenotype and viral-DNA results separate. Record all treated plants, early losses, survivors, and symptomatic survivors before interpreting a reported response percentage; never turn a survivor-based efficiency into natural-trait prevalence.

For a claimed named variegated cultivar, retain authenticated propagation provenance and compare serial sector distribution, leaf-age position, growth and pigment measurements under matched conditions; resemblance to Divina alone cannot authenticate cultivar or exclude infection.
Do not confirm genetic variegation, chimerism, mutation, virus freedom, or training ground truth from a photograph or video.
Record the exact leaf, node, branch, plant, cultivar, propagation source, date, stage, lighting, and serial change; include healthy plants of the same cultivar and environment.
Inspect both leaf surfaces and protected growth with magnification, and document pest organisms or their absence separately from the color phenotype.

Measure root-zone pH and EC and review irrigation, tissue or solution analysis, nutrient history, spray records, lamp position, temperature, and mechanical injury before assigning a developmental explanation.

Submit symptomatic and matched asymptomatic tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for a locally appropriate validated virus/viroid differential; a negative targeted assay excludes only the agents and sample covered by that assay.

Before destructive sampling, photograph and map pale and adjacent green sectors from the same leaf or branch separately; coordinate paired sampling with the laboratory and preserve individual plant, node, tissue, and assay identifiers rather than pooling away the boundary.
When a genetic attribution is operationally important, compare mapped sectors and clones and use qualified genetic or meristem-lineage analysis; persistence alone is supportive context, not proof.

Separate observations on originally affected leaves from new leaves and descendant shoots; record experimental manipulation history if present, but never infer TRV infection or a stable mutation from bleaching localization alone.

Track independently identified descendant cuttings under matched conditions and record both persistence and loss of the phenotype; do not infer seed inheritance, a stable cultivar trait, or transmissibility from one mother plant or cutting.
immediateActions: Keep the visual label at “chlorotic sectoring—cause unresolved” and flag it for human review.
Pause distribution of suspect cuttings and separate them from verified genetic-trait references until infectious causes are reasonably excluded.
Preserve serial imagery and matched tissue before pruning or discarding the affected shoot.
correctivePlan: Correct only measured root-zone, nutrient, pest, or exposure problems and document whether new growth changes.
If validated pathogen testing is positive, move the sample to the confirmed pathogen class and follow the facility’s sanitation and plant-health protocol.
If differential testing is negative and the pattern tracks a shoot or clone, retain a “suspected genetic/developmental” label unless genetic evidence supports a stronger claim.
prevention: Maintain cultivar, mother-plant, cutting-position, and clone-lineage records.
Use tested propagation stock and tool-sanitation practices so a stable-looking pattern is not assumed noninfectious.
Capture healthy reference plants under repeatable lighting and camera settings for color comparison.
warnings: The Divina/Pilar evidence here is limited to the public primary-study abstract; no full methods, item-level media rights or sample-level genetic confirmation was reviewed. Its authors attribute the selected phenotype to a spontaneous chimera, but no unknown plant inherits that causal label.

Lower growth in a documented variegated cultivar can be developmental context rather than proof of a new disorder, but this comparison cannot normalize new distortion, spreading chlorosis or unexplained decline; keep the infectious, nutritional and exposure differential active.

Neither pale-sector area nor resemblance to Divina establishes cannabinoid or terpenoid content, harvest maturity, cultivar identity, seed inheritance or a universal biomass penalty; unsupported causal or chemical labels require human review.

Image/video-only confidence is capped at 0.10 as a conservative annotation policy, not a measured accuracy estimate; visible sectoring remains a phenotype label until independently supported causal attribution.

The sequencing study used three stem positions on one Honey Banana mother plant, not paired pale and green leaf sectors; its variant counts cannot validate a sector label, predict potency loss, or establish inheritance.
“Genetic mosaicism” describes within-organism genetic variation; a visible “mosaic symptom” is not evidence of that mechanism.
The Cannabis mosaicism sequencing study sampled one mother plant and did not link its variants to visible leaf sectors.

The 2022 TRV study provides an experimentally induced look-alike, not field evidence of natural TRV disease; its largely leaf-localized response cannot establish spontaneous variegation, inheritance, or pathogen freedom.
The VIGS bleaching experiment was an intentionally virus-vector-induced gene-silencing phenotype and must not be treated as proof that natural bleaching is inherited or noninfectious.

The composite reference image mixes four unresolved mosaic-like presentations with panel e, which the authors characterize as somatic-mutation-associated chlorotic sectors; preserve panel labels and never train the entire composite as one genetic class.
Negative molecular, microscopy, or indicator-host findings are bounded by sample quality, agent coverage, assay performance, and observation time.
This reviewed record validates an uncertainty-bounded workflow, not image-only genetic ground truth; all symptom-only samples remain human-review items.

sources.title: Accumulation of somatic mutations leads to genetic mosaicism in cannabis
sources.publisher: Wiley on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America
supportedClaims: The Honey Banana study sequenced three stem samples at different heights from one approximately 1.5-year-old mother plant; it did not compare visibly pale and green leaf sectors or demonstrate a causal pigment mutation.

Deep whole-genome sequencing of top, middle, and bottom samples from one 1.5-year-old Cannabis mother plant detected many variants unique to individual canopy samples, demonstrating within-plant genetic mosaicism in that plant.
The study examined a single mother plant and did not validate a visible leaf-sector pattern as a diagnostic marker of somatic mutation, heritability, or clonal stability.

sources.title: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: Experimental silencing of Cannabis phytoene desaturase and magnesium-chelatase-subunit-I genes produced spotted leaf bleaching, 70–73% lower target-transcript expression, and corresponding carotenoid or chlorophyll-a reductions.

This deliberately induced, virus-vector phenotype shows that perturbing pigment-related gene expression can create visible bleaching; it does not establish that naturally occurring sectors are genetic or safe from infectious differentials.

In experimentally treated Finola, small white spots appeared on newly developed leaves approximately four weeks after treatment; neither PDS nor ChlI silencing produced completely bleached leaves. This is an induced, cultivar- and experiment-specific appearance, not a natural variegation timeline.

For PDS, 38 plants were treated, 13 died early, and five of 25 survivors showed bleaching; for ChlI, five of 23 survivors from 40 treated plants showed bleaching. The reported 20% and 22% efficiencies use survivor denominators, not all treated plants or field prevalence.

Five-week PCR detected both vector DNA components in empty-vector controls as well as PDS- and ChlI-silenced plants, although empty-vector controls lacked the bleaching phenotype. A green experimental control therefore cannot be relabeled pathogen-free from appearance or confused with an untreated wild-type control.

sources.title: Tobacco Rattle Virus as a Tool for Rapid Reverse-Genetics Screens and Analysis of Gene Function in Cannabis sativa L.
supportedClaims: The primary study abstract reports experimentally induced PDS-silencing photobleaching largely restricted to the treated Cannabis leaves despite limited vector spread; localized pigment loss therefore does not by itself establish a stable genetic trait.

The study concerns an engineered reverse-genetics system, not a survey of spontaneous Cannabis variegation or natural Tobacco rattle virus disease; its phenotype cannot establish natural infection, inheritance, or pathogen freedom in an unknown plant.

Figure 1 compares three Cannabis lines two weeks after experimental PDS silencing: a = MF-71, b = MF-169, c = MF-219, while d is an empty-vector control. Local bleaching was mainly vein-associated and varied among lines; the panels are not serial stages of one plant.

sources.title: Challenges to Cannabis sativa Production from Pathogens and Microbes—The Role of Molecular Diagnostics and Bioinformatics
sources.organization: International Journal of Molecular Sciences (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: The authors documented Cannabis leaves with mosaic, mottling, and line patterns that superficially resembled viral symptoms, and separately illustrated sharply chlorotic, chlorophyll-deficient sectors attributed to somatic mutation in Figure 4e.

Defined broad-spectrum and specific RT-PCR assays did not detect the targeted viruses in tested OG Kush and Headband tissues; positive controls worked, no virus-like particles were seen in the examined Cannabis samples by transmission electron microscopy, and inoculated indicator hosts remained symptomless for three weeks.

Those negative results apply only to the sampled tissues, agents, assays, and observation period and therefore do not establish genetic causality or exclude every virus, viroid, pest, nutrient, root-zone, or chemical cause.

Figure 19 documents indoor Cannabis plants with stunting, extensive young-leaf curling, and twisted or deformed stem growth plus outdoor plants from four genotypes with visibly different symptom presentations; BCTV presence was confirmed by RT-PCR with universal BCTV primers.

The Figure 19 asset is a multi-genotype, multi-setting composite rather than a panel-resolved progression series, so it supports visual context but not a universal phenotype or panel-level automated-training label.

sources.title: Cannabinoids and terpenoids yields of the ornamental Cannabis sativa L. cultivar 'Divina' characterized by a variegated foliage as morphological marker
supportedClaims: The publisher abstract describes variegated Divina as a cultivar selected from a spontaneous chimera detected in green-leaved Pilar. This is a named cultivar-lineage report, not proof that any visually similar Cannabis leaf has the same genetic cause or cultivar identity.

The abstract reports significantly lower leaf chlorophyll in Divina and generally slower growth and less biomass than Pilar when mother plants were grown under similar long-day conditions; the proposed chlorophyll-related explanation is presented as supposition, not a mapped causal mutation.

In a same-location comparison under artificial growing conditions, Pilar produced higher cannabinoid and terpenoid yields than Divina. Dataset annotation inference: this cultivar comparison does not validate a color-to-potency rule, chemical prediction from an image, or a universal yield penalty for spontaneous sectoring.
